voice: Blustering, patronizing, corrupt, and deliberately theatrical Irish-American detective; readable period speech with occasional Irish rhythm but no leprechaun vocabulary or dense eye-dialect.

entries.text: I've no use for that, Miss Bow.
Most definitely. I've put away more criminals this year than you'll see in your entire life.
You see it your way, lass, and I'll see it mine.
And where did you find that thing?
You haven't been disturbing evidence at crime scenes, have you, Miss Bow?
I should hope not. Tampering with evidence could put you in a great deal of trouble.
Good.
There's a man who doesn't know his head from a hole in the ground. Anyone who lets his newspaper criticize the police is downright addled.
Bifocals? I don't know about such things. I'm still a young man.
That's downright repulsive. Why would I know--or want to know--anything about a smelly old work boot?
If you ask me, they're blowing the whole thing out of proportion. You'd think something important had been stolen.
Listen, girlie, if I chased every petty theft among the city's less respectable elements, I'd be working thirty hours a day.
All right, no more 'girlie.' Miss Bow, then--when I remember.
I'd rather not be here at all, much less answering questions about something as silly as carbon paper.
He's got too many brains, that one. He thinks he's better than the rest of us.
Most of the furnaces in New York burn coal, missy. That's hardly worth writing home about.
I enjoy a bit of cheese now and then, but I'm not hungry. Find me later.
Now there's a slippery old bat. If she's royalty, then I'm Rudolph Valentino.
He's the pest who's always hanging around the station house. I thought he was supposed to cover this so-called event. No great loss.
It's an oversized letter opener, if you ask me.
See here, that's someone's private diary. You shouldn't be reading it.
Bones. Don't talk to me about bones. I've seen enough of the bloody things to last a lifetime.
The docks are dangerous, lass--as many cutthroats as rats. Stay away if you know what's good for you.
Enough to know Egyptology is a bloody waste of time. Sifting through old bones and rotting tombs--better to let the dead rest.
He's an all-right sort of fellow, I suppose. I haven't spent much time with him.
I appreciate a good garter as much as the next man, Miss Bow, but is this an appropriate subject?
I love grapes. They're good for the constitution and the circulation. Some people insist one kind is better than another, but I eat them all--seeds and everything.
He's not much of a security chief. A thief walked into his museum and stole an exhibit from under his nose--and Heimlich cannot account for where he was that night.
Don't waste your time on those Egyptian squiggles. They'll rot your brain.
I believe I've heard of your father. New Orleans, isn't it? They say he was pretty good, for a Southern policeman.
What possible use could a little slip of a girl like you have for a lantern that size?
They're good. They put exactly enough starch in my shirts.
Afraid of the dark, little girl? I don't blame you. New York can be a rough town.
He's an odd duck, but he presses my trousers exactly the way I like them.
Do you expect to find important clues with that little magnifying glass, missy? Let me know if you discover anything worth my time.
What's a nice girl like you doing with a piece of flesh?
It's tolerable, if you care for that sort of thing. I'd rather be at the station house with a drink and sensible company.
Of course it's the land of opportunity. Look at me--a detective in the finest city in the world.
You've got a little notebook. Isn't that precious? Solve the mystery of the missing letter opener and perhaps we'll make you an honorary policewoman.
That woman is downright unnatural, Miss Laura. Stay away from her. She keeps asking whether I have any scars.
Why, that's me, silly girl: Detective Ryan Hanrahan O'Riley, at your service.
That fellow is too big for his britches. Someone ought to take him down a notch or two.
I've better things to do than read the notes of an old pottery-chaser who ended up with a letter opener in his chest.
That's a fine pocket watch, Miss Laura. Shame it isn't running. Have you tried winding it?
New York's police force is the finest in the world. Don't you forget it, lass.
I hate press passes. Those little cards let nosy reporters interfere in our investigations whenever they please.
I don't like that fellow. Too soft for my taste, and far too interested in other people's business.
My hair has been red since the day I was born. Steve Dorian's is nearly the same shade, and several others here have red hair as well. It's a regular carrot-top convention.
That's one more bizarre object in a thoroughly bizarre place. I don't know what it opens, and I don't care.
Smelling salts aren't so popular now, but women used to carry them everywhere. I think half of them fainted simply so a man would catch them.
What in the world is that contraption? You are a strange young woman.
Selling snake oil is what this ridiculous museum does best.
Mark my words: I'll have every one of those dens of iniquity closed before the year is out.
He seems pleasant enough, but I wouldn't trust anyone from the docks. They're rough company for a young woman like you.
The Tribune is a nest of yellow journalists, young lady. You ought to find respectable work. Have you considered becoming a secretary?
Temper, temper, missy. I thought reporters were meant to remain objective.
I'd pay good money to see you in a catfight, lass. My money would be on you.
There's an odd one. The man comes from Egypt to recover his precious Dagger, and then someone steals it. Quite a coincidence--and he has very little alibi.
I don't know much about animal hair.
Do you always carry a water glass, Miss Bow? Were you lost in a desert as a child?
That's police business, girl. Keep your little nose out of it.
That's a dangerous character. Stay away from him. He eats little girl reporters like you for breakfast.
What on earth do you want to know about wire for?
A young woman like you ought to be thinking about marriage, not prowling around asking about burglary tools.
That charming Miss Yvette said she was missing a shoe. Perhaps it's hers.
Now there's a lovely woman. A genuine lady, if you take my meaning.
That man is a human weasel. Stay away from him.
How should I know? I'm a detective, not an encyclopedia. Ask something sensible.
I'm a busy man. Don't waste my time by asking the same question twice.
No, thank you. My eyes are perfectly sound.
I don't need that, girl.
What would I want with that?
No, thank you. I'll stick to my grapes.
That's the real Dagger. I'll take it into police custody now, if you please.
Thank you. I'll see that the evidence is kept safe.
Keep your hands to yourself, lass.
That's charming, but save it for somewhere more discreet.
Thank you, but those grapes don't look fresh.
I don't intend to explore any dark places, and neither should you.
Thank you, but I'm bright enough already.
Don't look at me like that. You're making me nervous.
I like my steaks rare, but no thank you. I'm watching my waistline.
I don't wear jewelry. It's a bit too fancy for a man, if you ask me.
I'm sure your notes are fascinating, but I'm conducting my own investigation in my own way.
What, do you think I can stick it back on?
Take that away. It's making me queasy.
I don't need that thing. I don't even know what it is.
Watch it. My stomach isn't happy; I think I ate a bad grape.
I don't have time for idle chat, Miss Bow.
Detective Ryan O'Riley, at your service. You're looking lovely this evening.
No, thank you.
I'm not thirsty, but thank you.
That's official police property. Give it here.
You're a violent little girl, aren't you?
I won't be needing that.
Nice girls shouldn't play with things like that. You don't know where it's been.
That's not mine. I believe it belongs to Miss Yvette.
A tall, red-haired detective surveys the room as though it belongs to him. His badge identifies him as Ryan O'Riley.
You should not be so interested in dead people, Miss Bow. You are beginning to sound like that morbid Dr. Myklos.
It could cost you your life.
There is a killer loose in this museum. If you keep putting your nose into his business, he may decide he dislikes the attention.
Certainly. If he believes you are on his trail, killing you would be one way to cover it.
So keep your pretty little head out of his business--and mine.
Of course. Dr. Myklos fetched me and said the Countess asked for me before she died. The strange part was how delighted Myklos seemed to find the old bat dying on her desk.
Did you find any clues?
No. This killer is a tricky one.
No. It is as though someone reaches every scene before me and removes anything useful. Either the killer leaves no clues, or someone is cleaning up after him. All I am left with is the body.
Do I tell you how to write your little articles? You have been a pain in my side all night. Stay out of police business, or I will put you in a cell and let you count the bricks.
Yes. My guess is that the poor fellow drank too much. There was enough alcohol on him to pickle a horse.
The man had many personal difficulties, from what I understand.
Do not be ridiculous. Obviously he climbed onto the tusks before he drank too much.
I have seen stranger things. I enjoy a drink myself from time to time.
Are you explaining the law to me, missy?
Hmph.
My guess is that someone grew tired of the man's enormous ego.
Anyone who met him. Carter was so full of himself there was scarcely room for another person nearby.
You discovered the body, silly girl. Someone put a dagger in his chest. That tends to kill a man.
The coroner attended the party. When he left, he took Carter's body with him--ego and all.
Yes.
We have a museum full of suspects. Everyone appears to have enjoyed Miss Delacroix's company, if you take my meaning.
There are as many motives for murder as there are words in the dictionary.
I am beginning to suspect two murderers. Fast-setting plaster might explain the timing, but coating and moving her body would be easier with two people.
Can you keep a secret, Miss Bow?
I should not say this, but I am suspicious of Myklos and Heimlich. She is altogether too fond of dead things, and he owns more books on torture than the public library.
I have been a policeman for a long time. A successful homicide investigation requires instinct as well as evidence, and my instinct points toward those two.
I suspect everyone--even you. Perhaps you are killing people to make a name for yourself writing about them.
I am making a point. Everyone has a motive once you learn enough about them.
Which piece? A little police humor.
I need a sense of humor in this work. Do you imagine I enjoy examining detached pieces of men I knew?
I do not. Whoever killed Ziggy was making a display of it: first pinning his body to the floor with a pterodactyl, then mounting his head.
There is nothing ordinary about this killer. He is clever, and it is almost as though he is toying with me.
Perhaps it is a warning not to interfere. Or perhaps the killer is simply a lunatic--a clever lunatic, but a lunatic all the same.
Certainly you have, Miss Bow. And I have just been appointed police commissioner.
Have you, now? Where did you find it?
It sounds as though you sampled the alcohol while you were down there.
Have you, now? Let me see it.
